tldr: This paper systematically evaluates whether widely accepted VLA inference techniques and data-collection tricks actually hold up across 100 diverse household tasks in BEHAVIOR-1K. The findings overturn common assumptions: shortening action chunks causes performance to plummet, while slashing denoising steps down to just a single step causes no performance drop at all.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which generate robot actions directly from vision and natural language, have attracted immense attention as the leading approach toward general-purpose robotics. However, a VLA model's success depends heavily not just on its weights, but also on runtime recipes: how many action steps to execute ahead during inference, how many denoising iterations to run, and how to efficiently collect recovery data after failures. The trouble is that most previously reported tricks were validated only on specific tasks, such as folding towels or single assembly jobs. It remained unclear whether they actually help across a broad range of tasks.

To address this gap, the authors conducted a rigorous, head-to-head comparison of inference and data-collection techniques proposed in prior work and competition-winning models across BEHAVIOR-1K, a challenging benchmark covering 100 complex household tasks. As their base model, they adopted $\pi_{0.5}$, a flow-matching VLA model fine-tuned based on the winning approach from the BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025.

The experiments uncovered several surprising facts. Halving the number of action steps executed at once (action-chunk execution horizon) caused the overall Q-score to drop sharply by 0.16. In contrast, reducing denoising steps from 20 all the way down to just 1 step resulted in zero performance drop. Furthermore, while resuming from snapshots of failed episodes cut simulation computation by 30% to 40%, it backfired unless the policy's internal belief state about its current task stage was restored as well. This practical and insightful study highlights that strategies proven on small-scale tasks do not necessarily transfer when brought to large-scale environments.
contributions: Conducted the first systematic, paired evaluation of inference settings and data-collection strategies for a VLA model ($\pi_{0.5}$) across all 100 tasks of the large-scale household robot benchmark BEHAVIOR-1K.
Demonstrated that shortening action-chunk execution horizons significantly degrades performance, whereas reducing denoising to a single step fully preserves performance.
Showed that resuming from snapshots of failed episodes cuts simulation steps by 29% to 43%, and discovered that restoring the policy's internal stage belief is essential when doing so.

sections.heading: Are Standard VLA "Secret Sauces" Truly General?
sections.summary: While VLA performance depends heavily on inference and data-collection settings, their efficacy has only been tested on narrow, specific tasks. This study conducts the first large-scale evaluation across 100 household tasks to test the generality of these common assumptions.
sections.details:
Unlocking the full potential of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models requires more than just pretraining and fine-tuning. The runtime settings chosen during inference and the strategies used to collect additional data are equally crucial. However, many settings used in practice have simply been carried over as-is from prior pipelines.

Prominent examples include the configuration used by Larchenko et al., the winners of the BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025; advantage guidance (a sampling technique that promotes desirable actions) proposed for garment folding; and inference settings reported for single-task industrial setups. Whether these recipes hold up across the full suite of BEHAVIOR-1K, which spans 100 diverse and complex household tasks, remained an open question.

To find out, the authors conducted a paired evaluation to settle the score on inference and data-collection settings across all 100 tasks with 4 instances each. The results revealed that halving the number of executed actions severely dropped the overall task achievement metric, the Q-score, by 0.16. Meanwhile, the 1.3x playback speed-up adopted by the winning team remained effective, and slashing flow-matching denoising from 20 steps down to 1 step caused no detectable drop in performance. For data collection, resuming from intermediate snapshots reduced computational cost by 29% to 43%.

sections.heading: Sorting Good Settings from Bad via Strict Paired Comparisons
sections.summary: Using a $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint based on the BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 winner, all 100 tasks were evaluated under official rules. To eliminate random noise, differences against the average of two baseline runs were judged using task-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals.
sections.details:
The base policy for the experiments uses $\pi_{0.5}$, initialized from the BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 winner's checkpoint. $\pi_{0.5}$ is a state-of-the-art VLA model based on flow matching, a variant of diffusion models that rapidly generates action trajectories from noise. It was fully fine-tuned on the BEHAVIOR-1K dataset, followed by a self-improvement loop: rollouts collected in training environments were filtered for successful and partially successful runs, then mixed with demonstration data for continual learning. In addition, each frame was assigned a RECAP-style binary advantage label indicating whether it contributed to success, enabling conditioned training.

Evaluation was conducted on the public test set across all 100 tasks of BEHAVIOR-1K under the same constraints as the official challenge. The primary metric was Q-score (0.39 for the baseline), which integrates task progress and success rate.

The key methodological choice here was the statistical approach used to catch subtle differences in inference settings. Two independent simulation runs served as the baseline (control group), and differences ($\Delta$Q) caused by each setting modification were computed. Furthermore, 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a task-clustered bootstrap. A setting was judged significantly beneficial or significantly harmful only when its confidence interval did not cross (did not include) zero. This robust experimental design avoids overreacting to mere fluctuations in mean values.

sections.heading: Overturning Common Wisdom: What You Can Cut and What You Can't
sections.summary: Shortening chunk length during inference severely hurts performance, yet cutting denoising to 1 step and disabling overlap inpainting had zero negative impact. For data collection, restarting right before task progress dropped proved effective, and restoring the policy's internal state was found to be indispensable.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Inference Ablations
The authors kept the model unchanged and compared variants by altering only how it was run during inference.

- Action-Chunk Execution Horizons: The model predicts a chunk of future actions, but this setting determines how many of those steps from the beginning are actually executed in the environment. Halving the horizon from the default 26 steps to 13 steps significantly degraded both Q-score and success rate, while increasing episode lengths. Frequent replanning likely causes the model to chase different strategies between consecutive chunks, leading to erratic behavior.
- Playback Speed-Up: The 1.3x playback speed-up used by the winning model performed clearly better than real-time (1.0x). Under strict episode time limits, packing more actions into the allotted time proved beneficial. However, pushing it to 2.0x showed a downward trend in performance (though not statistically significant), likely because motions became too crude.
- Denoising Steps: The number of generation steps varies widely across studies, from 4 steps in GR00T N1 to 10 steps in $\pi_0$. The authors reduced the count from their default of 20 steps to 10, and boldly down to just 1 step. Remarkably, no performance drop was detected. A single inference step is already sufficient to land right next to the intended action mode (the high-density region). This is a welcome finding that can drastically reduce inference compute costs.
- Overlap Inpainting: This interpolation feature smoothly blends with the previous chunk during asynchronous inference. Disabling it entirely showed no detectable difference in Q-score.
- Advantage-Guidance Strength: Increasing the weighting coefficient $\beta$ for desirable actions from the default 1 to 2 worsened scores, and setting it to 4 performed only on par with 1. Increasing it offered no benefit.

### 3.2 Data Collection
Ablations on recovery strategies designed to collect training data efficiently.

- Restart Points: When re-running a failed episode partway through, the authors compared where to resume. Restarting from the state right before predicted task progress first dropped produced trajectories that earned the highest progress scores.
- Simulation Cost: Resuming from snapshots cut simulation steps by 29% to 43% compared to simulating episodes from start to finish. However, it did not significantly increase the number of successes per simulation step.
- Stage-Belief Restoration: The winning $\pi_{0.5}$ model feeds its stage prediction—its belief about which phase of the overall task it is currently in—back into the next step. When only the simulation environment was rolled back while this internal stage belief was reset, Q-score and progress dropped substantially. Rolling back the policy's internal belief alongside the environment is essential.

sections.heading: New Guidelines for VLA Deployment Revealed by Large-Scale Testing
sections.summary: Large-scale testing across 100 tasks revealed that tricks effective on specific setups do not always generalize. Keeping action chunks sufficiently long, boldly cutting denoising steps, and preserving internal model state during rollbacks emerge as practical best practices.
sections.details:
This paper carried out an exhaustive audit of VLA inference and data-collection recipes at an unprecedented scale across all 100 tasks of BEHAVIOR-1K.

To summarize the takeaways: shortening action chunks breaks the policy's strategic consistency and should be avoided, while a moderate playback speed-up (1.3x) is beneficial. On the other hand, computationally heavy multi-step denoising and overlap inpainting can be trimmed without hurting performance. In data collection, snapshot restarts contribute substantially to saving compute, but the model's internal awareness of task phases (stage belief) must be restored consistently.

"A technique that works on one task may not function the same way when task difficulty and diversity scale up." Backed by solid experimental data, this study delivers a valuable and easily overlooked reminder for practical robotics.

takeaways: Inference denoising for flow-matching VLAs can be cut from 20 steps down to just 1 step with virtually no performance loss, offering huge potential for inference speedups.
Shortening the action-chunk execution horizon too much disrupts policy consistency across consecutive predictions and causes performance to plummet, meaning chunks must maintain adequate length.
When rewinding and resuming failed episodes, one must restore not only the simulator's physical state but also the model's internal belief state regarding task progress.
limitations: Evaluations were conducted strictly in simulation (BEHAVIOR-1K); it remains unverified whether the same inference settings are optimal under real-robot control latencies and hardware noise.
While snapshot restarts successfully reduced simulation steps, they did not lead to an increase in the final task success rate per simulation step.
